newsitem.title: COMOROS: OAU mission to Comoros raises hopes for compromise.
newsitem.headline: OAU mission to Comoros raises hopes for compromise.

text.p: An Organisation of African Unity (OAU) mediator will on Monday visit the Comoros second island of Anjouan where government troops were reported to have landed to quell a secessionist revolt.
Diplomats in the Comoran capital of Moroni said the OAU mission offered the first real chance to break through the wall of distrust between the government and the secessionists.

The OAU said last week that envoy Pierre Yere would discuss measures to defuse tension "while addressing the legitimate concerns of the islanders while maintaining the unity, territorial integrity and cohesion" of Comoros.
Foundi Abdallah Ibrahim, 75, who leads the secession demand, was declared "president" of Anjouan by a crowd of islanders last week.

Anjouan islanders demand a return to French rule, saying they have experienced nothing but poverty and political unrest since the main group of Indian Ocean islands declared themselves independent in 1975.

The poverty in the independent Islamic Republic of the Comoros contrasts with the comparative prosperity on the adjoining island of Mayotte, which voted against independence in 1975 and remains French.
Journalists on Anjouan reported on Saturday that a small number of soldiers landed there before dawn in an attempt to quell the secessionist protests.

Details were scarce, but residents said Ibrahim's bodyguards on Saturday seized three government soldiers who they said had attempted to enter his residence, and paraded the soldiers before crowds of elated islanders.
Yere, the Ivory Coast's ambassador to Ethiopia, who arrived in Moroni on Saturday, said Comoran government leaders had told him they had sent no troops to Anjouan.
Yere did not travel to Anjouan on Sunday, as planned, and said he would go on Monday.
He held meetings in Moroni on Saturday with Comoran president Mohamed Taki and members of his government.

To the annoyance of the Comoran islanders, local broadcasts of programmes from French radio and television stations have been cut, and the official Comoran radio has made no mention of the Anjouan crisis.

One islander said Anjouan was "awash with rumours" and the situation was tense. On Moheli, a smaller island which also has a strong independence movement, demonstrators supporting Anjouan's secessionists set up road blocks.
France has refused to support the secessionists, saying the Anjouan situation is serious and could destabilise the whole region.
Three people including a gendarme were killed on July 14 -- Bastille Day -- as demonstrators, pressing for Anjouan to return to French rule or be independent, clashed with security forces.
